techniques.name: Permutation Tests
techniques.description: A permutation test asks how likely an observed result would be if there were no real relationship in the data. The tester shuffles the data many times in a way that breaks the relationship under test, recalculates the metric each time, and takes the p-value as the share of shuffled results at least as extreme as the real one. Shuffling the outcome labels and retraining tests whether a classifier's accuracy beats chance, and shuffling group membership tests whether a gap between groups in the rate of decisions, such as approvals, is larger than chance would produce. A restricted variant, Ojala and Garriga's second test, shuffles each feature's values separately within each class, which keeps every feature's own spread but breaks the relationships between features, so a classifier that makes significantly fewer errors on the real data than on the shuffled copies is using those relationships. The test needs no assumption about the shape of the data's distribution, but a small p-value does not show that an effect is large, important or causal.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital research group trains a classifier on 80 patients with thousands of gene-expression measurements. With so few cases, a good cross-validated accuracy could be luck, so it repeats the whole training and testing procedure on thousands of label-shuffled copies and reports the result only if it beats nearly all of them.

A council analytics team replacing a case-prioritisation model checks whether the new model's higher accuracy on the same test cases could be chance. It randomly swaps the two models' predictions case by case 10,000 times, recomputes the gap each time, and switches only if the real gap is larger than nearly all of the shuffled ones.

A bank's model-risk team sees a higher approval rate for one applicant group than another in a loan model's decisions. Before escalating, it shuffles group membership across applicants thousands of times and recomputes the gap, to test whether a gap this large could arise by chance. A significant gap prompts a fuller review but does not by itself show unlawful discrimination.

A cardiology team using a gradient-boosted model to flag high blood pressure expects height and weight to matter together, not only alone. It shuffles each feature within each outcome class 1,000 times and tests at the 5% level whether the model errs less on the real data, to decide if a simpler model treating features separately would do. A non-significant result means either the features are unrelated within classes or the model ignores the relationship.

limitations.description: Each permutation needs the metric recalculated, and a model may need retraining every time, so thousands of permutations of a large model can be expensive. Stricter thresholds need more permutations, because the smallest possible p-value is 1 divided by the number of permutations plus one, and repeated runs can disagree near the threshold.

Assumes exchangeability of observations under the null hypothesis, which may be violated in time series or hierarchical data structures, where simple shuffling gives p-values that are too small or too large.

A significant result shows that the data are unlikely under the stated null, such as 'features and labels are independent'. It does not show that the effect is large, important or causal, and shuffling cannot rule out a confounder or an artefact of how the data were collected.

Testing many features or groups at once produces some false positives by chance, so the p-values need correcting, for example with a false discovery rate procedure. Without that, a feature-by-feature test over many features will flag some that are only noise.

What is shuffled defines the question answered. Shuffling labels tests whether features and labels are related at all, while shuffling features within classes tests whether a classifier uses dependencies between features. The wrong scheme answers a different question from the one the assurance claim needs.

resources.title: Significance Tests Which May be Applied to Samples from Any Populations
Permutation Tests for Studying Classifier Performance
resources.abstract: We explore the framework of permutation-based p-values for assessing the behavior of the classification error. In this paper we study two simple permutation tests. The first test estimates the null distribution by permuting the labels in the data; this has been used extensively in classification problems in computational biology. The second test produces permutations of the features within classes, inspired by restricted randomization techniques traditionally used in statistics. We study the properties of these tests and present an extensive empirical evaluation on real and synthetic data. Our analysis shows that studying the classification error via permutation tests is effective; in particular, the restricted permutation test clearly reveals whether the classifier exploits the interdependency between the features in the data.

resources.title: Nonparametric permutation tests for functional neuroimaging: A primer with examples
resources.abstract: Requiring only minimal assumptions for validity, nonparametric permutation testing provides a flexible and intuitive methodology for the statistical analysis of data from functional neuroimaging experiments, at some computational expense. Introduced into the functional neuroimaging literature by Holmes et al. ([ 1996 ]: J Cereb Blood Flow Metab 16:7–22), the permutation approach readily accounts for the multiple comparisons problem implicit in the standard voxel‐by‐voxel hypothesis testing framework. When the appropriate assumptions hold, the nonparametric permutation approach gives results similar to those obtained from a comparable Statistical Parametric Mapping approach using a general linear model with multiple comparisons corrections derived from random field theory. For analyses with low degrees of freedom, such as single subject PET/SPECT experiments or multi‐subject PET/SPECT or f MRI designs assessed for population effects, the nonparametric approach employing a locally pooled (smoothed) variance estimate can outperform the comparable Statistical Parametric Mapping approach. Thus, these nonparametric techniques can be used to verify the validity of less computationally expensive parametric approaches. Although the theory and relative advantages of permutation approaches have been discussed by various authors, there has been no accessible explication of the method, and no freely distributed software implementing it. Consequently, there have been few practical applications of the technique. This article, and the accompanying MATLAB software, attempts to address these issues. The standard nonparametric randomization and permutation testing ideas are developed at an accessible level, using practical examples from functional neuroimaging, and the extensions for multiple comparisons described. Three worked examples from PET and f MRI are presented, with discussion, and comparisons with standard parametric approaches made where appropriate. Practical considerations are given throughout, and relevant statistical concepts are expounded in appendices.

sample_claims.text: The classifier's accuracy on the patient cohort exceeds what label-shuffled copies of the same data produce, at the 1% significance level

techniques.name: Differential Privacy Auditing
techniques.description: Differential privacy auditing tests whether a training procedure that claims a differential privacy guarantee at a stated budget (epsilon, where smaller means stronger privacy) loses more privacy in practice than the claim allows, by measuring a statistical lower bound on its true epsilon. The guarantee itself comes from a mathematical proof, and membership inference testing reports attack success on real records for any model; the audit instead controls which records are present and asks whether the code that was run honours the proof, so it can expose an implementation bug or accounting error but can never confirm the guarantee. The auditor builds two training sets that differ only by one or a few planted records, called canaries and often crafted to be easy to detect, trains the model many times on each, and applies a fixed test to every trained model to guess whether the canary was present. Confidence intervals for the test's true-positive and false-positive rates, such as Clopper-Pearson intervals for a proportion, are converted into a value of epsilon that the procedure must exceed at a stated confidence level, such as 99 per cent; a bound above the claimed epsilon shows that the claim is false for that implementation. Because hundreds of training runs are costly, a later design needs only one: many canaries are each included or left out at random, the test guesses which were included, and the share of correct guesses gives the bound, which is looser than the many-run design's.

example_use_cases.description: Before an NHS trust releases a readmission-risk model trained with an open-source differential privacy library at a claimed epsilon of 3, its data science team audits the exact code and settings: it trains several hundred models with and without a planted mislabelled record and signs off only if the 99 per cent lower bound stays below 3, recording that the audit could have caught a violation but cannot prove the guarantee.

The maintainers of a differentially private training library run a white-box audit on every release: the auditor sees each intermediate model update and inserts a gradient crafted to be easy to detect, so a change to the clipping or noise-sampling code that silently weakens the guarantee pushes the lower bound above the budget the library reports and fails the build.

A mobile keyboard team training a next-word model with federated learning under a claimed user-level guarantee adds simulated canary users to its single production training run, each included or left out at random and enough of them that a bound above the claim is reachable, and checks the one-run lower bound against the claim, because retraining the federated model hundreds of times is not feasible.

limitations.description: A result below the claim proves nothing. The bound is only as strong as the audit behind it: weak canaries, a test that sees only the final model, or too few runs or canaries can give bounds far below the claimed epsilon (one library's documented single-run audit with 1,000 canaries reported 0.42 for a model trained at epsilon 68.5, and 5.5 for one trained without differential privacy). Only a bound above the claim is conclusive, and a pass must not be reported as confirming the guarantee.

The number of training runs caps what can be detected. With 500 runs per training set and 99 per cent confidence, the largest bound the original method can report is about 4.5 even if the test never errs, so it cannot show a claimed epsilon of 8 to be false; larger budgets need many more runs or a different design. In the single-run design the number of canaries sets the cap in the same way.

Bounds come close to the claim only under the strongest access. For DP-SGD on natural data, audits match the claimed epsilon when the auditor sees every intermediate update and inserts crafted gradients, the setting the standard proof assumes. With crafted input records, seeing every update helps only slightly over the final model, and with the final model most of the original audit's bounds were roughly 7 to 12 times below the claim. A result holds only for the access and canaries it assumed.

It is expensive. The original method trained 500 models per training set to choose the test's threshold and another 500 per set to estimate its error rates, which is impractical for large models. The single-run design avoids this but gives looser bounds, which weaken further when only the final model is seen and the model cannot memorise all the canaries or other training data is added.

It checks one implementation, configuration and pair of datasets. A change of clipping norm, batch size, random initialisation or library version needs a new audit, and canaries that are typical rather than worst-case can miss a violation that affects only unusual records, giving false confidence about the risk to outliers.

resources.title: Auditing Differentially Private Machine Learning: How Private is Private SGD?
resources.abstract: We investigate whether Differentially Private SGD offers better privacy in practice than what is guaranteed by its state-of-the-art analysis. We do so via novel data poisoning attacks, which we show correspond to realistic privacy attacks. While previous work (Ma et al., arXiv 2019) proposed this connection between differential privacy and data poisoning as a defense against data poisoning, our use as a tool for understanding the privacy of a specific mechanism is new. More generally, our work takes a quantitative, empirical approach to understanding the privacy afforded by specific implementations of differentially private algorithms that we believe has the potential to complement and influence analytical work on differential privacy.

techniques.name: Kernel Two-Sample Test (Maximum Mean Discrepancy)
techniques.description: A kernel two-sample test checks whether two sets of data could have come from the same distribution; in assurance it is used to check whether the inputs a deployed model now receives still resemble the data on which it was validated, and to detect when they stop doing so. Its statistic, the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), is built from a kernel, a function that scores how similar two data points are (commonly a Gaussian function of the distance between them), and in its usual squared form it is the average similarity among points in the reference sample, plus the average similarity among points in the new sample, minus twice the average similarity between points from different samples. With a characteristic kernel such as the Gaussian, the population value is zero only when the two distributions are identical, so the test can respond to any kind of difference, including a change in how features vary together that tests applied to one feature at a time cannot see, and kernels exist for strings and graphs as well as numerical vectors. To obtain a p-value, the two samples are pooled and repeatedly divided at random into groups of the original sizes, the statistic is recomputed for each division, and the p-value is the share of divisions giving a value at least as large as the one observed; high-dimensional inputs such as images are usually first reduced to a short vector, for example the code of an autoencoder or the model's predicted class probabilities. The output, for each window of new data, is the MMD value and its p-value at a stated significance level, which shows whether that window differs detectably from the reference, but not whether the difference affects the model's accuracy.

example_use_cases.description: A card issuer's model-risk team tests a random sample of each night's transactions, at most one per customer, against a fixed sample from the fraud model's validation period, after standardising the input features. It set the significance level so that, with nothing changed, it expects about one false alarm a quarter, and a significant result triggers a check of the model's accuracy on newly labelled cases before its alert thresholds are relied on the next day.

Before switching on a chest X-ray triage model at a second hospital that uses a different make of scanner, the deploying team compares 500 recent images from the new site with 500 from the validation set. Each image is first reduced to a short vector by an autoencoder trained on validation images. A significant difference sends the model for local validation on labelled cases from the new site instead of relying on its original results.

A customer-service team whose question-answering assistant was evaluated on a fixed test set compares the sentence embeddings of each week's user questions with those of the test set. When a week is flagged, it computes the MMD witness function, which scores each question by how much more it resembles the new week's questions than the test set, reads the top-scoring questions, finds queries about a new product, and adds such questions to the test set.

limitations.description: A significant result shows that inputs differ from the reference, not that the model has got worse: Rabanser et al. note that distributions shift constantly and often harmlessly, and with large windows the test can flag differences too small to matter. A drift alarm becomes evidence about performance only when followed by an accuracy check on labelled cases, and an absence of alarms reassures only if the test was shown beforehand to detect the shifts that harm the model.

On raw high-dimensional inputs the test has little power: in Rabanser et al.'s comparison on image data the multivariate test performed poorly without first reducing the dimension. The reduction then decides what can be seen, since a change that leaves the autoencoder code or predicted probabilities unchanged goes undetected. The kernel's width matters too: it is usually set to the median distance between points, which Gretton et al. call a heuristic, the best width being an open question.

The statistic compares every pair of points, so its cost grows with the square of the combined sample size, and the permutation test repeats it many times; Rabanser et al. ran kernel tests only up to 1,000 new samples for this reason. Gretton et al.'s linear-time version is far cheaper but needs much more data for the same power, so high-volume monitoring has to trade window size, detection delay and computing cost against each other.

The permutation p-value assumes that observations within each sample are independent. Consecutive sensor readings, transactions from one customer or successive time steps are correlated, and shuffling them breaks that dependence, so the test signals a difference far more often than its stated level: in Chwialkowski et al.'s experiments on autocorrelated signals the permutation test almost always rejected when nothing had changed. Such data need thinning or a wild bootstrap.

Run on every new window at the conventional 5 per cent level, the test flags about one window in twenty even when nothing has changed, which for daily windows means around 18 false alarms a year. Continuous monitoring needs a stricter level, a correction for repeated testing, or an online version of the test whose threshold is set for an expected run time between false alarms.

resources.title: A Kernel Two-Sample Test
resources.abstract: We propose a framework for analyzing and comparing distributions, which we use to construct statistical tests to determine if two samples are drawn from different distributions.  Our test statistic is the largest difference in expectations over functions in the unit ball of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), and is called the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD).  We present two distribution-free tests based on large deviation bounds for the MMD, and a third test based on the asymptotic distribution of this statistic.  The MMD can be computed in quadratic time, although efficient linear time approximations are available.  Our statistic is an instance of an integral probability metric, and various classical metrics on distributions are obtained when alternative function classes are used in place of an RKHS.  We apply our two-sample tests  to a variety of problems, including attribute matching for databases using the Hungarian marriage method, where they perform strongly.  Excellent performance is also obtained when comparing distributions over graphs, for which these are the first such tests.

Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift
resources.abstract: We might hope that when faced with unexpected inputs, well-designed software systems would fire off warnings. Machine learning (ML) systems, however, which depend strongly on properties of their inputs (e.g. the i.i.d. assumption), tend to fail silently. This paper explores the problem of building ML systems that fail loudly, investigating methods for detecting dataset shift, identifying exemplars that most typify the shift, and quantifying shift malignancy. We focus on several datasets and various perturbations to both covariates and label distributions with varying magnitudes and fractions of data affected. Interestingly, we show that across the dataset shifts that we explore, a two-sample-testing-based approach, using pre-trained classifiers for dimensionality reduction, performs best. Moreover, we demonstrate that domain-discriminating approaches tend to be helpful for characterizing shifts qualitatively and determining if they are harmful.

sample_claims.text: Applied to autoencoder representations of 500 images from each source, the kernel two-sample test found no significant difference at the 1 per cent level between the new hospital's chest X-rays and the validation images, and the same test detected the simulated scanner changes that had reduced the model's accuracy in validation.

Every alarm raised by the nightly kernel two-sample test on the fraud model's inputs in the past six months was followed within two working days by an accuracy check on newly labelled cases, and each check either met the accuracy requirement or led to retraining.

In each weekly window since deployment, the loan-application model's production inputs showed no difference from its validation sample detectable by the agreed kernel two-sample test, at a significance level corrected for weekly repetition, and the same test detected the input shifts that had reduced the model's accuracy in pre-deployment trials.
Replayed on reference data alone, the drift monitor's kernel two-sample test raised false alarms at no more than the configured rate of one per quarter.
